For hours, the cold, hypnotic blue light of the computer screen had been my entire world. Seeking a way to break free from its spell, I stepped outside and began to climb a steep, unpaved mountain road. The path was overgrown with wild, jagged thistles that scraped against my ankles through my pants—a sharp, physical sting that served as a subtle, transformative shock to my system. It was precisely the kind of harsh, unscripted reality I needed to sever the thread binding my mind to the digital void.

Before escaping outdoors, my entire day had been consumed by a desperate, mechanical ritual. I had spent hours obsessively checking stock market data, refreshing charts with the frantic compulsion of an addicted gambler standing before a slot machine. Every red drop in price brought a wave of nausea; every flash of green brought a fleeting hit of dopamine. I was trapped in a cycle of waiting, endlessly hoping that the numbers would shift in my favor and transform my precarious investments into sudden, comforting profit.

Yet, even out here in the wilderness, the obsession proved difficult to shed. As I pushed higher up the trail, the natural landscape began to warp, intertwining strangely with my financial anxieties. The mountain wind no longer sounded like pure nature; instead, it felt charged with invisible data. I imagined stock tickers, crypto algorithms, and fluctuating world currencies drifting through the pine-scented breeze, casting a ghost-like overlay onto the pristine forest. The jagged ridge line of the peaks looked suspiciously like a volatile market chart, proving that my mind was still tethered to the very systems I was trying to escape.

As the physical exertion deepened, so too did my inner turmoil. A profound existential conflict raged within me. Part of my brain was consumed by a dark, apocalyptic dread—a conviction that the world was teetering on the brink of economic and environmental collapse, rendering all human ambition futile. Yet, paradoxically, another part of me gripped onto a fierce, almost absurd optimism: a desperate desire for personal longevity, a wish to live a long, prosperous life and reap the rewards of a future I wasn't even sure would exist. 

Standing near the summit, looking out over the vast valley below, I questioned my profound inability to simply remain steady. I longed for calm, yet I realized that tranquility was foreign to me. My only true sense of balance did not come from a peaceful middle ground, but from the chaotic collision of these extreme moods. I was a creature powered by contradictions—holding dread in one hand and hope in the other—finding a strange, precarious equilibrium only when the world around me felt as volatile as the storm inside my head.

The monitor hums in the quiet room, casting a cool, relentless glow across my desk. On screen, a jagged constellation of red and green line graphs updates in real time, a hypnotizing, dopamine-dappled ledger of micro-fortunes made and lost by the second. My eyes track every flicker, every sudden dip and violent spike, bound to the screen by a feverish, addictive compulsion. My pulse vibrates in rhythm with the market’s volatility, each fraction of a percentage point feeling like a life-or-death judgment. To look away is to miss the signal; to keep looking is to slowly shred my own nerves.

Beyond the frame of the glass, visible through the nearby window, the asphalt of a narrow mountain road begins its steep ascent, carving a path out of the valley and disappearing into the shadowed, granite folds of the forest. The idea of standing up, closing the laptop, and stepping out into that landscape presents itself not just as a choice, but as an exorcism. I imagine trading the dry heat of the computer fan for the bite of cool alpine air, replacing the frantic, silent chaos of the ticker with the rhythmic crunch of gravel underfoot and the steady, demanding exertion of climbing. Perhaps, I think, the sheer physicality of the mountain can ground a psyche currently spinning out of orbit.

Yet, as I stare at the road rising toward the treeline, I realize that the mountain is not an escape from my mind, but a larger mirror for it. The obsession with the market is merely a symptom of a much deeper, violent division within my own soul. I do not live in the present; I live at the intersection of two wildly exaggerated futures.

On one side lies a dark, paralyzing apocalyptic dread. When the line on the screen plunges, it feels like the herald of a grand collapse—not just of an index, but of civilizational infrastructure, of safety, of meaning itself. In those moments, I am convinced that ruin is the only logical conclusion to human ambition, and I wait for the end with a mixture of terror and dark anticipation.

On the other side lies a blinding, utopian hope. A sudden surge in the charts brings with it visions of total transcendence—a future where all scarcity is conquered, where control is absolute, and where life unfolds in a state of frictionless, golden harmony. I build entire arcadias out of a few green candles, convinced that perfection is just beyond the next resistance level.

I am perpetually torn between these two poles, swinging wildly from the brink of total annihilation to the heights of unimaginable paradise. I tell myself that I want the peace of the mountain, a quiet center where the storm clears and stillness takes over. But the truth, laid bare in the quiet contemplation of leaving my desk, is far stranger: I do not know how to exist in the middle ground. 

If I walk up that mountain road, I will not find a tranquil mind waiting for me at the summit. I will simply take my chaos into the wilderness. My sense of balance does not come from the absence of turmoil, but from its terrifying abundance. I am kept upright only by the equal and opposite pressures of my own extreme impulses—the apocalyptic and the utopian slamming into one another at full speed, canceling out total madness with equal parts terror and wonder. The collision of these chaotic extremes is my only version of equilibrium, a precarious, vibrating tightrope suspended over the abyss.

There is a rare and glowing window in the turning of the year when the world seems entirely renewed. It arrives with the height of **May**, when the earth casts off the last cold whispers of winter **and** steps fully into the light. The hedges are thick with hawthorn blossom, the woods are carpeted in bluebells, **and** the air carries the sweet, heady scent of life in full bloom. 

As nature reaches this brilliant crescendo, traditional calendar celebrations offer a rhythm to match the season. Among the most cherished of these is **Whitsuntide**, the historic festival of Pentecost. Falling in the late spring, Whitsuntide has long served as a bridge between the quiet promise of early spring **and** the golden abundance of summer. 

Historically, this was a time of bright new beginnings. In villages across the countryside, Whitsuntide brought Whitsun walks, brass bands playing on town squares, **and** children dressed in crisp white clothes to symbolise purity **and** rebirth. Village greens blossomed into life with Maypoles **and** Morris dancers, their bells jingling in rhythm with the spring breeze. It was a holiday meant for step-singing, outdoor feasting, **and** gathering under an open sky, celebrating both spiritual renewal **and** the warmth of the returning sun.

The beauty of **May** **and** **Whitsuntide** lies in how seamlessly they intertwine. Nature provides the breathtaking backdrop—the canopy of fresh green leaves **and** the long, gentle twilights—while Whitsuntide provides the human chorus of gratitude **and** joy. Together, they remind us to pause, step outside, **and** welcome the light. 

To walk through the meadows during this magical time is to feel grounded in history **and** lifted by the present. **May** brings the blossoms, **Whitsuntide** brings the song, **and** together they create a timeless celebration of hope, community, **and** the enduring majesty of the natural world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short stream-of-consciousness prose poem about a day trader attempting to escape screen addiction by hiking a mountain, blending market anxiety with vivid natural imagery.
counterfactuals.output: Step, step, double-top, the tree roots cross the dirt like broken trendlines, I left the six monitors humming in the air-conditioned dark but the retinas—god, the retinas keep printing. *Buy the dip, short the ridge, limit order at the treeline.* Every ponderosa pine is a long green candle stretching toward a sky that won’t stop bleeding blue light. My pocket heavy with the dormant phone—was that a vibration? No, just salt-sweat trickling down my thigh, just the ghost-thumb twitching for glass, starving to swipe open the atmosphere, to check if the forest is outperforming the morning index. Pulse at 160 BPM, *tick, tick, tick*, volume surging in my throat, breath coming as thin and brittle as liquidity in an August flash crash. Higher now. The granite path steepens into a vertiginous resistance level, sheer rockface, zero leverage, unhedged gravity where one missed footing means total portfolio liquidation. *Don't look back, don't check the bell.* The wind rattles through the aspen leaves like a trillion micro-transactions executed in a fraction of a millisecond, a chaotic order book tumbling through the valley, but the mountain sits indifferent, holding its position for ten thousand years. Scramble over the final slate ledge, hands torn, knees scraped—shorting the valley, longing the peak—and suddenly the horizon ruptures wide, an uncapped, unquantifiable expanse of wild earth where no algorithm can follow, burning out the phantom wicks behind my eyelids until there is only the blinding, quiet, un-monetized sun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a manic, dense postmodern passage set on May 23, 2010. Include themes of stock market addiction, negative theology, fields of thistles, and an existential crisis about emotional volatility.
counterfactuals.output:
May 23, 2010—Pentecost Sunday, appropriately, though the only wind blowing through this degraded bypass lot behind the Mahwah data centers is a hot, particulate gale smelled faintly of diesel and ozone, and I am sitting tailor-fashion in a sprawling, aggressive colony of *Cirsium arvense*—Creeping Thistle, prickly, invasive, its spiny pappus clutching at the hem of my trousers like jagged little barbs of bad debt—staring into the blue-lit quartz face of a Blackberry Bold 9700, waiting for the Globex Sunday night futures open at 18:00 EST, because seventeen days ago the Dow dropped nearly one thousand points in thirty-six minutes (the May 6 Flash Crash, a trillion-dollar phantom limb amputated by Waddell & Reed’s algorithmic sell order, an unscheduled descent into the abyss from which no price discovery could save us) and my central nervous system has not reset its margin requirements since. 

I am twitting, twitching, adjusting my posture on the dry dirt among the violet-headed thistles whose sharp, stiff bracts seem to mimic the intra-day tick charts of the VIX—the volatility index, the fear gauge, the terrifying math of human panic made actionable—and I am paralyzed by the suspicion that my soul is fundamentally high-frequency; that my affect is no longer a human rhythm but an automated execution loop, a series of microsecond sentiment swings completely divorced from macroeconomic realities or basic emotional fundamentals. Why did I weep at a billboard for an LG washer at 2:14 PM, only to feel an icy, triumphant euphoria at 2:16 PM? What fundamental catalyst justified that re-rating of my internal equity? There was no news on the wire! No revision to my life’s GDP! Just a sudden, un-hedged cascade of neurotransmitters, a fat-finger trade in the limbic system that wiped out three months of steady, cognitive-behavioral gains before the circuit breakers could even trip. 

And isn’t this, really, the supreme apophatic truth? Isn’t the market—and by extension, the Divine—defined strictly by what it *is not*? Negative theology for the hyper-leveraged age: God is not the Bid, God is not the Ask, God is not the underlying asset, nor the yield curve, nor the Eurozone bailout package currently rotting in Brussels while Greece burns. God is the void between the trades, the dark liquidity pool, the absolute silence of the un-executed limit order, the Un-Tick. Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite sits on a Bloomberg Terminal in 5th-century Syria and types: *The Supreme Cause is neither light nor dark, neither green candle nor red, but an incomprehensible darkness of un-pricing.* To pray is merely to refresh the app; to worship is to hold short positions on your own serotonin while the thistles prick through your socks, reminding you that nature, too, is just a ruthless, un-hedged hedge fund choking out the gentler flora through brutal, spiky expansion.

The sun is dipping behind the server farms—those anonymous, windowless gray cubes housing the black-box algorithms that execute arbitrage off the millisecond delay caused by the speed of light travelling through fiber-optic cable under New Jersey asphalt—and I am thumbing the trackball with a frantic, calloused digit, skin peeling, heart racing at 130 beats per minute on no coffee, just pure, unadulterated speculative terror. The futures are about to open. If the E-mini S&P opens down six handles, I am ruined; if it opens up four, I am merely doomed to stay awake until the Tokyo session opens at 20:00. My emotional baseline is an unviable derivative product. I prick my finger on a thistle’s needle—a sharp, sudden spike of localized pain, a tiny red dot blooming on my thumb like a real-time price tick—and I cannot tell if I am a man experiencing an existential breakdown in a weed-choked field, or merely a glitching trading bot, perpetually bidding up its own suffering in a market that closed long before the world was even made.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece of experimental fiction in the style of Ben Lerner that contrasts the manic energy of day-trading with the quiet grandeur of a sea-view summit?
counterfactuals.output:
I had attained the ridge—a granite spine jutting six hundred meters above the Pacific, which from this vantage presented less as water and more as an unblinking, slate-gray eye—not to commune with the sublime, but because the cellular tower mounted near the fire lookout offered five bars of ultra-low-latency 5G. 

My thighs burned from the steep ascent through the chaparral, a dull, lactic throb that felt absurdly anachronistic, a pre-digital bodily residue, while in the palm of my right hand, held at an angle to deflect the blinding, unmediated glare of the sea-light, a green-and-red visualizer of high-frequency liquidity pool imbalances refreshed every two hundred milliseconds. 

I was long on forty zero-day-to-expiration SPX call options. 

To stand on the summit was to experience a profound spatial deceleration. Below me, the ocean churned against the basalt headlands in slow, ancient iterations, a blue-black engine of deep time operating on a scale that rendered human history an unnoticeable smudge on the geology. The wind smelled of crushed sage and cold salt. It was the classic landscape of Romantic self-effacement—the kind of vista designed to make the observer feel beautifully, poetically small. 

Yet my thumb was performing a frantic, micro-choreography across the gorilla glass. 

Within the warm enclosure of the screen, a completely different regime of scale was unfolding—one of hyper-compressed, panic-adjacent velocity. The Federal Reserve Chairman had just opened his mouth at a press conference in Washington, three thousand miles away, and the market was undergoing a violent, algorithmic spasm. A single phrase regarding neutral interest rates had triggered an avalanche of automated sell orders. On my screen, the green candlestick I had been tracking—a fragile vertical representation of collective optimism—collapsed into a long, weeping red line. 

I was losing four hundred dollars every three seconds. 

The contrast produced a strange, somatic dissonance, a vertigo that was neither entirely physical nor entirely conceptual. I looked up: a red-tailed hawk glided on a thermal, perfectly motionless, suspended in an ocean of cool air, entirely indifferent to the collapse of regional banking equities. I looked down: the bid-ask spread was widening with terrifying, predatory speed, market makers withdrawing liquidity into the ether, leaving my position stranded like a sea creature caught in a sudden, artificial low tide. 

I tried to synthesize the two experiences, to construct a meta-narrative in which the erratic movements of the market were simply an extension of natural forces—a weather system of late-capitalist affect, as indifferent and majestic as the Pacific. But the metaphor failed instantly under the weight of its own bad faith. The sea was indifferent because it possessed no consciousness; the market was a hyper-conscious, hyper-mediated feedback loop composed entirely of human terror and greed, abstracted through mathematical models designed to extract value from time itself.

"Are you taking a photo?" 

I turned. A hiker had materialized behind me, wearing a synthetic moisture-wicking shirt and carrying a wooden walking stick. He looked serene, healthy, fully integrated into the narrative of the mountain.

"No," I said, my voice sounding thin and raspy, the voice of a man who had forgotten he possessed a larynx. "I’m attempting to liquidate a leveraged bet on the short-term direction of the American economy before my capital is entirely destroyed."

The hiker smiled uncertainly, assuming I was executing a piece of dry, urban ironism, and stepped past me to admire the horizon. "Incredible view," he murmured. "Makes you realize how small all our problems are."

"If this position expires out-of-the-money," I said to his back, "I will be unable to pay my rent in Brooklyn."

He did not reply. He simply took a deep breath of the pine-scented air and allowed the silence of the summit to wash over him.

On my screen, the red line reached a floor. A sudden, massive inflow of volume—a whale, or perhaps a consortium of quantitative hedge funds responding to a secondary interpretation of the Fed Chairman’s syntax—entered the market. The candlestick reversed. It did not merely recover; it shot upward in a vertical green spike that breached the upper Bollinger Band, an event of pure, unadulterated speculative mania.

In forty-eight seconds, I went from a net loss of two thousand dollars to a net profit of four thousand six hundred. 

My heart was hammering against my ribs, a manic, Tachycardic rhythm that matched the screen’s pulse, totally divorced from the quiet, rhythmic respiratory needs of a body sitting on a mountain. I swiped my thumb across the glass, executing the order. *Filled.* The trade was closed. The unrealized gain became realized capital, a string of digits translated into a database in New Jersey.

I tucked the phone into my pocket. 

Suddenly, the screen's glow was gone, replaced by the crushing, absolute silence of the afternoon. The wind rustled the scrub oak. The ocean glittered below, vast, indifferent, and completely unaffected by the four thousand six hundred dollars I had just abstracted from the collective panic of the globe. 

I stood there for a long time, waiting for the manic energy to subside, for my nervous system to recalibrate to the deep, slow time of the granite and the sea. But the calm refused to arrive. The summit remained magnificently mute, and I felt only the profound, hollow exhaustion of a man who had traveled to the edge of the world merely to watch a light turn green.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explore the idea of a person whose "only balance is built of collisions" using motifs of financial ticker symbols, redtail hawks, global currencies, and apocalyptic light.
counterfactuals.output:
He does not know the stillness of a plumb line or the calm of a quiet room. If you froze time, he would fall over like a bicycle at a red light. His spine is a pendulum that only stays upright when struck; he is a violent gyroscope, kept vertical by the precise, relentless friction of opposing forces. 

His fulcrum is impact. 

Look at him standing on the lip of the glass-and-steel ruin, silhouetted against a sky painted in apocalyptic light—a bruised, radioactive violet bleeding into sulfur-orange, the kind of light that signals either the end of a world or the dawn of a deeply hostile one. The sun is a swollen, dying dwarf, casting crepuscular rays like fractured spears through the ozone haze. 

Above him, the sky is not empty. A single redtail hawk hangs in the violent updrafts of the burning canyon. The bird is an avatar of his internal physics. It does not fly by resting on the air; it rides the turbulence where cold atmospheric fronts slam into the searing heat rising from the asphalt below. It balances on the edge of a stall, its feathers shuddering in the crosswinds, its golden eye locked on the earth. Its entire existence is a high-speed negotiation with gravity—a controlled fall, a strike, a violent rebound. The hawk stoops—falling like a stone, speed compounding until it collides with a thermal, snapping its wings wide to turn a lethal plunge into a violent, breathtaking ascendance. 

```
[MARKET STATUS: CRITICAL]
$USD/JPY: 154.20 ▼ 12.4%  |  $EUR/USD: 0.88 ▲ 4.1%
$REDT/HWK: STOOP AT 120MPH |  $GLOB/PAIN: OVERBOUGHT
```

Inside the man’s chest, the arithmetic is identical to the markets crumbling around him. He is a walking exchange rate, a human clearinghouse where trauma is converted into kinetic energy. He counts his pulse not in beats, but in tick-data, his nervous system flickering like an arcade screen running out of power:

`$STRIKE` `▲ 14.8`
`$FRACTURE` `▼ 2.1`
`$SURVIVE` `[VOLATILITY HIGH]`

He lives in the spread. When the world collapsed, when the global reserve currencies began to melt into history, he was the only one who didn't lose his footing. Why would he? He was already built on insolvency. 

He remembers the sound of the old world dying in the exchange rates: the frantic sell-offs of the Japanese Yen (`JPY`), the paper-thin collapse of the Euro (`EUR`), the quiet evaporation of the Indian Rupee (`INR`) and the Nigerian Naira (`NGN`). When money lost its static value, when the dollar (`USD`) became nothing more than kindle for campfire light under a dying sun, people who needed stability went mad. They had relied on the myth of the solid floor. 

But he had always lived on the trading floor of catastrophe. 

When a shockwave hits him—a literal blast of wind from the burning lowlands, or the memory of a past life catching him in the ribs—he doesn’t brace. He pivots. He absorbs the momentum. He uses the left-hook of the world to swing his right foot forward. 

```
[EUR/JPY] -> UNBALANCED
[INR/USD] -> LIQUIDATED
[KINETIC/EQUILIBRIUM] -> ABSOLUTE
```

The light shifts. The sky breaks open in a silent, EMP-tinted aurora, casting stark, razor-sharp shadows across the cracked concrete. It is light from a dying atmosphere, illuminating the absolute truth of his mechanics: *To stand still is to die; to be struck is to step.*

The redtail hawk swoops down low, passing close enough that he can hear the sharp *whirr* of air parting around its primary feathers. The bird collides with a sudden shear-wind, violently tossed ten feet sideways, but its head remains perfectly stationary in mid-air, fixed on its target. It uses the violence of the sky to keep its eyes level.

The man smiles—a thin, cracked line illuminated by the end-of-days glow. 

He steps off the ledge. 

He doesn't fly, and he doesn't fall. He catches the air like the hawk, trading speed for angle, collision for altitude. He lands on the fire escape three stories down with a bone-jarring impact that would break a static man. But the shock travels up his shins, through his hips, into his spine, recalibrating his inner ear, setting his compass, driving him forward into a sprint.

`$RDTL` `STOOP`
`$SOUL` `MARGIN CALL CLEARED`
`$BALANCE` `[ESTABLISHED VIA IMPACT]`

Around him, the currencies of the old world drift in the apocalyptic breeze—useless paper, digital ghosts of zeroes and ones. But he is fully solvent. His ledger is written in bruises, his net worth calculated in momentum. He is the only upright thing in a falling world, held high by the very things trying to tear him apart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a creative scene: A man sitting on a summit road with his laptop, compulsively checking stocks, wondering why he can't step into the wild landscape right in front of him.
counterfactuals.output:
The air at nine thousand feet was thin enough to burn the throat, sharp with the scent of crushed pine and sun-baked granite. Below the turnout, the world fell away into a jagged amphitheater of blue-mist valleys, ancient spires of spruce, and a sky so vast it felt like a weight pressing down on the crown of the head. 

Julian sat on the dusty gravel of the shoulder, his back resting against the front tire of his idling SUV. Across his thighs sat his warm, humming laptop, its screen a blinding rectangle of crisp LED light against the wild, untamed daylight.

*Refresh.*

Red. A drop of 1.4% in tech futures. 

*Refresh.*

Green. A slight bounce in his high-yield ETF. 

His index finger twitched over the trackpad like a nervous habit he’d inherited from a stranger. The battery was at twelve percent. His phone, propped against a rock beside him, was acting as a warm, straining hotspot, blinking heroically against the weak cell signal bouncing off a tower twenty miles down the canyon.

He had driven four hours up the winding, double-yellow rib of the mountain road specifically to leave it all behind. His boots were laced. His backpack, heavy with water and a folded trail map, sat in the passenger seat. The edge of the wilderness—the literal threshold where the gravel gave way to soft, pine-needle earth—was less than three feet from his left knee. 

All he had to do was stand up. Step over the invisible line. Walk into the trees where there were no tickers, no pre-market trading, no relentless, cascading waterfalls of red and green numbers claiming to represent the sum total of human value.

He raised his eyes from the screen. 

The view was stupendous. A red-tailed hawk glided on a thermal, effortless and suspended, completely unconcerned with interest rate hikes or quarterly earnings reports. The wind roared softly through the canyon, sounding like the ocean, whispering ancient, indifferent things to the cliffs.

Julian stared at the treeline. *Just stand up,* he told his legs. *Close the lid.*

His body refused the command. It wasn’t physical fatigue; it was a strange, terrifying vertigo. 

Out there, in the green and granite, there were no metrics. There was no real-time validation, no illusion of control. Out there, a storm was just weather, a bear was just a predator, and time moved at the agonizingly slow pace of decaying wood and growing moss. The forest didn't care about his portfolio. It offered no yield. It promised nothing.

The screen, by contrast, was a tether. It was a chaotic, bleeding mess, but it was *his* language. The green spikes gave him a hit of dopamine; the red dips gave him a spike of adrenaline. It made him feel like he was standing on the bridge of a ship, steering through a storm, even though he was just a man sitting in the dirt with cold hands.

He looked down at his leather dress shoes—he’d forgotten to change into his hiking boots before leaving the driveway—now coated in a fine layer of mountain dust. 

*Refresh.*

The market was closing in forty minutes. A volatile day. If he walked away now, if he lost service under the canopy of Douglas firs, he wouldn't know. He wouldn't be able to rebalance. He wouldn't be able to cut his losses. He would be entirely, helplessly present.

And the present terrified him. The present was nine thousand feet of empty air and a heart that pounded too fast in his chest.

A sudden gust of wind caught the top of his laptop screen, pushing it forward an inch. Julian flinched, snapping his hands out to save it, his heart jumping into his throat as if he’d almost slipped off the cliff itself.

He held the laptop tight against his chest, breathing heavily. He looked up at the mountains, then down at the screen. 

A low-battery warning popped up in the center of a candlestick chart: *10% remaining.*

Julian sat frozen on the razor's edge between the asphalt and the earth, waiting for the battery to die, hating himself for needing the machine to make the choice for him. 

*Refresh.*
